newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defense budget draws quick fire.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defense budget draws quick fire.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday proposed a $265 billion 1998 military budget that put off key decisions on force levels and arms modernisation and drew immediate fire from congressional Republicans.

The request for defence spending authority in the fiscal year beginning next Oct. 1 is a key part of Clinton's $1.69 trillion federal budget and includes a portion of a $3.5 billion payment to keep U.S. troops in Bosnia for 18 months.

"This budget request looks like a tightrope without a safety net," said House of Representatives National Security Committee Chairman Floyd Spence of South Carolina, who with other Republicans is concerned about recent defence budget cuts.

The Republican-controlled Congress wants at least $6.8 billion more for defence in 1998 but Defence Secretary William Cohen said Clinton's plan was sufficient and key strategy decisions could wait until completion of a Quadrennial Defence Review due within months.
"We can afford to do this at this point given the fact that we have seen a reduced threat from the former Soviet Union," Cohen told a Pentagon news conference.

"There are other types of threats emerging but this budget will get us to that process," he added, referring to a decision on whether troop totals will be slashed below the 1.44 million level to save money for weapons modernisation.

Despite a drive by Clinton and Congress to slash spending and balance the federal budget early in the 21st century, the defence request is likely to spark a fight with Republicans who worry that military spending has dropped dangerously.
Representative Curt Weldon, a Pennsylvania Republican, said the 1998 budget did not even approach providing the $60 billion a year for weapons modernisation requested by top military officers.

Cohen noted that the budget provides for a 2.8 percent military pay raise but suggested he might later ask Congress for a new round of military base closings to save money. He conceded it would be a difficult political issue because of the financial effect on the communities involved.

The $265 billion request compares to defence spending authority of $262 billion in current fiscal 1997. Defence spending authority includes additional money for projects that will continue over several years.

Congress has added billions of dollars to each of Clinton's defence requests and is likely to add money again this year. Congress had already allotted $272 billion for defence for next year in the budget resolution it approved last year, $6.8 billion more than Clinton's new request.

Defence officials said they expected protests over the size of the Bosnia request -- $1.5 billion in the budget plus $2 billion to be requested separately -- although Congress seldom rejects money for troops already committed abroad.

Clinton's budget includes $3.5 billion for anti-missile defences but only for development of a U.S. missile defence that could be built by 2003, rather than firmly committing to such construction as congressional Republicans want. But in a concession to lawmakers it would speed delivery of advanced battlefield anti-missiles like those used in the Gulf War.
The budget also includes $3 billion for development of a new attack submarine by General Dynamics Electric Boat Division and the Newport News Shipbuilding and Drydock Co.
